summary.text: Emancipation generally means freeing a person from slavery, indentured servitude, guardianship, or other restraints or legal disabilities imposed by a social system or legal code.
In a legal sense it is an act that sets free someone once under another's authority, and more broadly it means gaining economic, social and political rights and equality.
The word comes from a Latin term for liberating a child from parental authority, which in turn stems from a phrase meaning to capture from someone else's hand.

paragraphs.heading: Being set free
paragraphs.text: Emancipation, in its general sense, means freeing a person from some kind of restraint. That restraint might be slavery or indentured servitude, or it might be guardianship. It can also be any other limit or legal disability that a social system or a body of law places on someone.

paragraphs.heading: A word with a history
paragraphs.text: The word goes back to Latin. There, ēmancĭpo and ēmancĭpatio named the act of releasing a child from the authority of a parent. That Latin term itself grew out of the phrase ē manu capere, meaning to capture from another person's hand. People often treat emancipation and liberation as meaning the same thing, though scholars have drawn distinctions between the two.

paragraphs.heading: Legal and wider senses
paragraphs.text: In law, emancipation is the act that frees a person who used to be under someone else's authority from that authority. In a broader way, the word describes a group gaining economic, social and political rights and equality. Often it is used for a group that had been shut out from those rights. The phrase political emancipation is heard less often in modern speech, especially outside academic, foreign or activist circles, but similar ideas may go by other names.

paragraphs.heading: From abolition to civil rights
paragraphs.text: The United States offers an example of how the wider sense works. There, the Civil Rights movement culminated in three laws: the Civil Rights Act in 1964, the Voting Rights Act in 1965 and the Fair Housing Act in 1968. Together, these laws can be read as carrying further what began a century before with the Emancipation Proclamation and the end of slavery. In the islands of the British West Indies, both current and former, people mark Emancipation Day as a holiday celebrating the end of the Atlantic slave trade.

paragraphs.heading: Identity politics
paragraphs.text: Emancipation can also be tied to politics built around group identity. Emancipatory identity politics has been described by some as essentialist. So the word stretches from a child freed from a parent's authority, to people freed from slavery, all the way to identity politics.
